newsitem.title: USA: US economy seen slower but degree still a question.
newsitem.headline: US economy seen slower but degree still a question.

text.p: July U.S. trade data reported on Wednesday added another arrow to the quiver of evidence that the economy will decelerate in the second half of the year but the configuration and degree of that slowing is not yet fully defined, economists said.

"I think the economy during the second half of the year is probably growing at something around 1.5 percent," said Elliott Platt, managing director of economic research at Donaldson, Lufkin & Jenrette. "If you'd asked me yesterday, I'd probably have given you a figure like 1.7 or 1.8 percent."
The spur for Platt's slightly more subdued forecast for second-half-of-the-year economic growth was the surprising fall in the volume of U.S. exports in July.

While Platt's forecasts are on the weak side of Wall Street's gross domestic product (GDP) forecasts, economists agreed that the huge jump in the U.S. trade gap in July to $11.68 billion from a revised $8.19 billion in June provided another element of weakness to the U.S. economic picture.
The other parts of the economy contributing to the slowdown scenario are first and foremost, slower consumer spending, economists agree.
Consumption accounts for nearly two-thirds of all GDP and retail sales were relatively sluggish in June, July and August," observed Samuel Kahan, president of A.S.K. Financial Research Ltd.
Economists said that should come as no surprise after brisk consumer activity in the first two quarters of the year.

"After a strong burst of consumer spending in the first half of the year, the consumer taking a little time to catch his breath is not shocking and does not change the prospect for good, solid consumer spending going forward," said Charles Lieberman, chief economist at Chase Secuities.
Lieberman's growth forecast is more buoyant than Platt's. He sees 2.5 percent GDP growth in the third quarter and 3.3 percent growth in the fourth.
But temporary or more long-lasting, consumers are not the only ones taking their feet off the economic gas pedal.

"There's a slowdown in business spending on plants and equipment, a slowdown in government spending and there's been no significant bounce in inventories outside of the auto sector," said Platt. "And it's also the assumption that a wide trade deficit will detract from GDP."
Housing activity, also, has flattened, economists noted.
Economists estimate housing starts, to be reported on Thursday, totaled an annualized 1.445 million in August, down a bit from an annualized 1.46 million starts a month earlier.

"Our general view is that growth in the second half of the year is likely to remain somewhat stronger than the 2.0- to 2.5-percent sustainable growth path that the Federal Reserve is trying to get us back to," said Dana Johnson, head of research at First Chicago Capital Markets.
Johnson said before the July trade data were released, he estimated forecast growth of "around three percent for the third quarter and a little slower in the fourth quarter."

"To me, the key aspect of the data was the exports," said Johnson. "Export growth has been trending lower for about a year, suggesting that final demand from foreigners for U.S. goods is weakening. That will help slow the U.S. economy.
"That slowing trend is likely to turn around as growth in Mexico, Canada and Japan reaccelerate, but it's certainly not evident yet in the data," Johnson said.

Meanwhile, the wider July trade deficit "is a good reason to shade economic growth the forecasts a bit lower," Johnson said. "It is just one month's data, but it definitely argues for the notion that growth is moderating."
